title: Why Two Quotes for the Same Web App Can Be $60,000 Apart

The practical takeaway Web Development Software Development Startup Product Management Budgeting Why Two Quotes for the Same Web App Can Be $60,000 Apart Mohsin Arshad 3 min read · Oct 22, 2026 -- Listen Share Scope, hidden line items and hourly rates explain most of the gap. Here is how to compare quotes properly. Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by Mikhail Nilov on Pexels You send the same feature list to two development teams. One comes back at $35,000. The other says $95,000. Neither team is necessarily wrong, and neither is necessarily ripping you off. They are usually pricing different things. Almost every big gap comes down to three questions: what is in scope, what is included, and who is doing the work. 1. Scope is measured in hours, not features A “user dashboard” can mean one page with four numbers, or a configurable workspace with filters, exports and role-based views. Both fit in the same bullet point on a feature list. One takes a few days. The other takes weeks. The simplest honest way to price a web app is: Estimated hours × blended hourly rate + a 10 to 20 percent change buffer If one team estimates 400 hours and another estimates 900 hours for the “same” app, the real conversation is about what each of them imagined you meant. Ask both teams to list their assumptions per feature. The gap often shrinks fast once everyone is describing the same product. 2. Some quotes leave out half the work A complete web app budget includes discovery, UI/UX design, frontend and backend development, integrations, QA, deployment and project management. A cheaper quote sometimes covers development only. Testing, cloud setup or design then show up later as change requests. Before you compare numbers, line the quotes up against that list and mark what each one actually includes. 3. Rates vary more than most founders expect Clutch’s pricing research shows most software development companies on its platform charging between $25 and $49 per hour, with clearly higher bands in North America and Australia. The same 600-hour project costs about $30,000 at $50 per hour and about $90,000 at $150 per hour. A lower rate is only a saving if the team also communicates clearly, tests properly and delivers on schedule. Rework is the most expensive line item in any project, and it never appears in the original quote. So what does a web app actually cost? As a rough guide for a professional team in 2026: Simple web apps, MVPs and internal tools: about $15,000 to $40,000, often in 6 to 10 weeks Medium apps such as customer portals with payments and integrations: about $40,000 to $100,000 Complex platforms such as multi-tenant SaaS or marketplaces: about $100,000 to $250,000 Enterprise systems with heavy compliance and legacy integrations: $250,000 and up Then add the cost nobody puts on the first slide. Maintenance and support usually run 15 to 25 percent of the build cost every year, before hosting and third-party services. The practical takeaway Do not pick the lowest number. Pick the quote whose assumptions you understand. Start with a focused first release, write your scope down before development begins, and budget for maintenance from day one. I wrote a longer breakdown with cost tiers, the seven factors that move the price most, a table of ongoing costs and an FAQ on the Infigo Solutions blog: Web Application Development Cost in 2026: Full Pricing Guide .
